newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German plan to revalue gold attacked.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German plan to revalue gold attacked.

text.p: Germany's controversial plan to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves to plug a hole in the budget deficit ran into massive criticism on Friday.

The proposal by Finance Minister Theo Waigel to revalue the central bank's gold holdings was widely denouced as hypocrisy in Germany and in some European countries, where memories linger of Waigel's stern warnings against such budgetary sleight-of-hand.

"With an arrogant style Waigel has accused other European countries of manipulating their budgets to meet the Maastricht criteria," said Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier, finance expert for the opposition Social Democrats. "Now he is pulling the same stunt."

Germany has been strongly against any kind of budget fudges for European economic and monetary union (EMU), but record unemployment which may average 4.3 million in 1997 has left Bonn struggling to meet the entry criteria.
The Maastricht Treaty says countries joining EMU should have budget deficits no higher than three percent of gross domestic product and overall debts not more than 60 percent of GDP.

Newspapers called Waigel's plan an act of desperation. They said it was a one-time budget accounting fudge that would neither help the economy nor solve any of the government's long term deficit problems.

Peter Struck, parliamentary leader for the SPD, said it was wrong to tamper with the Bundesbank's gold reserves. "We will suddenly be rich through tricks and manipulation. That is the same thing we have been labelling creative accounting by the Italians and Greeks," he said.
A key economic adviser to the government, Rolf Peffekoven, said revaluing the gold reserves carried inflation risks and should be seen as a measure never to be repeated.
Peffekoven, a member of the Council of Economic Advisers known as the "Five Wise Men", said the government should use only a small part of any revaluation windfall for budgetary ends.

Waigel, faced with an 18 billion mark ($10.6 billion) tax revenue shortfall, said on Thursday that if gold reserves were revalued from current low book prices to levels close to the normal market price it could help close the gap.
A revaluation would effectively deliver Bonn a windfall profit, allowing it to retire billions in old debt.
Government coalition sources said that members of the central bank have concerns about whether the plan to revalue the gold and foreign currency reserves could be implemented in 1997.
Germany currently values its 95 million ounces of gold at 144 marks per ounce -- well below the market price of 600 marks.

The mass-circulation Bild newspaper said Waigel's plan to lift the gold's value to near market prices amounted to "witchcraft". "The Waigel miracle -- a billion-mark hole disappears over night," Bild said.

The business daily Handelsblatt also criticised the plan. "The budget fever of the last days is shameful for a state of the economic ranking of Germany," the paper said in an editorial. "It disturbs the citizens, drives away companies and frightens investors."
Likewise, Die Welt said the plan "hurts confidence in the stability structure" of Germany.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini warned the plan could jeopardise EMU.

"I would be very surprised if the German government were to have recourse to accounting gimmicks such as the use of asset sales or a revaluation in order to meet a revenue shortfall for 1997," he told the International Herald Tribune.
A German currency expert slammed the plan as "cooking the books" and said the move could be unconstitutional.

Wilhelm Hankel, a former economics and finance ministry adviser, told the Berliner Zeitung daily that if a listed company were to behave in the same way it would lose all credibility with the banks and its shareholders.

"This would be cooking the books. Any private company that manipulates its profit figures loses the confidence of the banks and its shares collapse. What the German government is planning is no different," Hankel said.
